questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a glaze produces depth of colour
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a transparent glaze deepens a colour beneath it
questions.stem: During a survey of painted panels in a store, a technician examines a panel where the green drapery looks darker and richer than the pigment alone would suggest.

options.text: A transparent glaze of a deeper colour was laid over the light one, deepening it toward the dark.
The drapery was painted with more oil than the rest of the picture, so it reads richer.
options.misconception: attributes the depth to the oil medium in the paint

options.text: The panel was stored in dim light, so the drapery appears darker than it is.
options.misconception: blames the survey lighting for the apparent depth

options.text: The drapery was repainted, and the newer layer is simply better made.
options.misconception: assumes the depth comes from a later repainting

questions.explanation: A glaze is a transparent film that changes how the layer beneath is seen, so a deep green over a light one deepens it. Oil, lighting and repainting are separate things and do not produce that optical effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the transparent layer does to the colour below.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the difference a warm ground makes to a measured mixture
questions.stem: A survey team measures a grey mixture laid over a warm red ground at 18 per cent reflectance and the same mixture over a neutral ground at 30 per cent. By how many percentage points do the two readings differ?
questions.explanation: The two readings are 30 and 18, so they differ by 30 minus 18, which is 12 percentage points. This is the measure of how far the warm ground pulls the mixture away from its value on a neutral ground.
questions.hint: Subtract the lower reading from the higher one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sfumato changes in a face
questions.learningObjective: Identify what sfumato changes at the edge of a modelled form

stimulus.body: The survey record notes that the flesh of a face in one panel has no hard contour at the edge of the cheek, and that the tones change gradually over a distance of several millimetres, so that no line marks where the cheek ends.

questions.stem: According to the survey record, what has been changed in the rendering of this face?

options.text: The shadows have been painted grey, so the face looks flat rather than modelled.
options.misconception: reads the soft tone as a loss of modelling

options.text: The hard boundary of the tone has been dissolved, so the form turns without a drawn line.
The highlights have been left as bare ground, so the skin is warmer than the dress.
options.misconception: assumes the soft effect comes from exposed ground

options.text: The features have been shifted outwards, so the head is larger than life.
options.misconception: mistakes the soft edge for a change in proportion

questions.explanation: The record describes a gradual change of tone with no contour, which is the effect of sfumato, where the edge of a form is softened. Grey shadows, bare ground and shifted features are not what a soft boundary means.
questions.hint: The record says there is no line at the edge.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pentimento evidences
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a pentimento establishes about a painting's making
questions.stem: A conservator on the survey team is asked in writing what a pentimento can establish about a painting.

answer.exemplar: A pentimento is the earlier version of a passage that shows through the finished layer, usually where a later correction in an opaque paint covers an earlier one that was thinner or of a different colour. Its presence proves that the artist changed the design in the course of work, and it can show the direction of that change, the original placement of a figure or the first intention of a passage before it was revised.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines the pentimento as an earlier version surviving under a later one, and explains that it evidences a change made during the work. It should not present it as a signature, a date or a separate painting.
questions.hint: Say what is underneath and what was changed.

questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a craquelure network as evidence about film and support
questions.stem: The survey photographs a panel and finds that the cracks form a regular network of small cells, each about 4 mm across, concentrated in the sky and absent along the panel's edges.

options.text: The network shows where the panel was struck and cracked in a single impact.
options.misconception: explains the cells as impact damage

options.text: The network records splits that follow the wood's grain and run in one direction.
options.misconception: reads a random network as grain-following splits

options.text: The network is typical of an aged film that has dried and shrunk unevenly over a firm ground.
The network was drawn by a later restorer to imitate the look of an old picture.
options.misconception: suggests the craquelure is decorative imitation

questions.explanation: Small regular cells across the paint but not the edges point to a film that has shrunk and hardened over a stable support. Grain splits, an impact and painted imitation all predict patterns unlike this one.
questions.hint: Consider what the pattern does at the panel's edges.

questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Identify the evidence that a varnish was applied later
questions.stem: A survey team must decide whether the yellowed film on a panel is an original varnish or a later addition, given that the yellowing is heaviest where the panel is handled.

options.text: Concluding that it is later, because original varnish is always clear and colourless.
options.misconception: believes an artist's varnish must be colourless

options.text: Concluding that it is original, because varnish always turns yellow over a century.
options.misconception: assumes age alone proves the varnish is original

options.text: Concluding that it is original, because handling lifts a varnish evenly across a panel.
options.misconception: claims handling affects varnish evenly

options.text: Concluding it is later, because an artist's varnish would not be heaviest where the panel is handled.

questions.explanation: A later varnish is renewed where the picture is touched, so yellowing concentrated at the points of contact points to a later campaign. Age, even handling and a rule about clear varnish do not explain a patchy pattern.
questions.hint: Ask where the yellowing is heaviest.

questions.stem: A survey team compares a panel and a canvas. On the canvas, the drawn lines follow the weave and break where the threads rise.

options.text: The canvas is a newer support, so the broken lines prove the drawing is a later copy.
options.misconception: treats broken lines as evidence of a later copy

options.text: The weave of the canvas interrupts the stroke, so the line is broken and the drawing has a different texture.
The canvas holds less colour, so the artist had to draw with a thinner line.
options.misconception: blames absorbency for the broken line

options.text: The weave is coated, so the line stops wherever the coating is thickest.
options.misconception: explains the broken line by coating thickness

questions.explanation: A toothy, woven support catches the point and interrupts the stroke, so the same drawing reads differently on canvas than on a smooth panel. Age, absorbency and coating thickness do not explain lines that stop at the weave.
questions.hint: Watch the point of the tool at the threads.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a glaze produces depth of colour
questions.learningObjective: Compute the combined thickness of a glaze and the paint beneath it
questions.stem: A survey team measures a glazed passage with a depth gauge. The glaze film alone reads 0.06 mm and the paint beneath reads 0.12 mm. What is the total film thickness in millimetres?
questions.explanation: The total film is the glaze plus the paint beneath it, so 0.06 plus 0.12 gives 0.18 mm. Adding the two readings, rather than taking the larger, gives the thickness of the whole film.
questions.hint: Add the glaze reading to the paint reading.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a warm ground alters the hue of paint above it

stimulus.body: The note records that a panel was prepared with a warm brown wash across the whole field before the figures were painted, and that a face left thinly painted in the same medium as the figures appears warm and modelled, while the same mixture over the wash appears grey.

questions.stem: According to the note, what does the warm brown wash do to the colour painted over it?

options.text: It seals the panel so that the grey mixture cannot soak into the ground at all.
options.misconception: claims the wash stops the paint from sinking

options.text: It darkens the paint uniformly, so the grey mixture simply appears a deeper grey.
options.misconception: treats the wash as a uniform darkening only

options.text: It shifts the hue of the paint above it, since the wash shows through the thinner passages.
It adds a glossy surface that reflects more light back towards the viewer.
options.misconception: describes the wash as a reflective glaze

questions.explanation: Where the paint is thin, the warm ground shows through and shifts the hue of the mixture, which explains the warm flesh and the cool grey. Uniform darkening, sealing and gloss do not change hue.
questions.hint: Think about where the paint is thin.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a pattern of cracks in a paint film can show
questions.stem: A survey report asks in writing what a pattern of cracks in a paint film can tell the team about the object.

answer.exemplar: A network of small cells in the paint film shows that the film has aged, hardened and shrunk at different rates over a support that held it fairly steady, and the pattern of the cracks can be matched against the movement of the support. Cracks that follow the grain, cracks that open at a joint and cracks radiating from a point of impact tell the team about the movement of the wood, a weakness in the construction and a blow, each a different history from simple ageing.

questions.explanation: A good answer describes a pattern as evidence of how the film and support moved, and distinguishes ordinary ageing from structural faults. It should not treat every crack network as a single cause.
questions.hint: Different crack patterns mean different histories.

options.text: The underdrawing was copied from a print that showed a tower.
options.misconception: claims the underdrawing was copied from a print

options.text: The panel was cut from another picture that had a tower on it.
options.misconception: suggests the panel was cut from a larger composition

options.text: The tower is a later addition made after the picture was finished.
options.misconception: treats the tower as a later addition

options.text: The artist first included a tower and later painted it out, and the earlier version survives beneath.

questions.explanation: A form in the underdrawing, absent from the paint but visible in the film, is a change made during the work. A cut-down panel, a later addition and a copied print would not leave that stack of evidence.
questions.hint: Compare the drawing with what is painted there.

questions.topic: How a glaze produces depth of colour
questions.learningObjective: Choose the best treatment for a failing glaze over sound paint
questions.stem: A surveyor must choose the best treatment for a panel whose dark glaze has become dull and uneven, and whose paint beneath is sound.

options.text: Strip the glaze entirely and repaint the whole passage in the same glaze colour.
options.misconception: recommends stripping the glaze across the whole passage

options.text: Clean the surface gently, then renew the glaze only where the film is missing, matching the original layer.
Apply a fresh heavy glaze over the entire panel to even out the appearance.
options.misconception: advances adding a heavy glaze over everything

options.text: Wash the panel with solvent until the glaze is even, without further treatment.
options.misconception: advises solvent washing to even the glaze

questions.explanation: A sound paint layer under a failing glaze calls for cleaning and local renewal. Stripping, flooding with new glaze and washing alone all add or remove material needlessly.
questions.hint: Protect the sound paint layer beneath.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a softened shadow boundary changes a modelled face
questions.stem: A survey team records a face where the shadow beside the nose has no edge and fades over several millimetres into the lit cheek.

options.text: The shadow has been painted in a warm colour, so it does not look like a shadow at all.
options.misconception: explains the soft shadow by its colour

options.text: The shadow has been painted too lightly, so the face looks unfinished and needs more contrast.
options.misconception: reads soft shadow as an unfinished passage

options.text: The shadow has been softened into the light, so the form of the cheek turns without a drawn contour.
The shadow has been thinned with varnish, so it spreads across the surrounding paint.
options.misconception: blames varnish thinning for the soft shadow

questions.explanation: A shadow with no edge that fades gradually is sfumato, the softening of the boundary between tones so the form turns without a line. Unfinished contrast, warm colour and thinned varnish would each look different.
questions.hint: Look for the place where the shadow stops being a line.

questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Compute the mean yellowing index from four survey readings
questions.stem: A survey team measures the yellowing index of varnish on a panel at four places. The centre of the field reads 1.2, the upper edge 3.0, the lower edge 3.2 and a point beside the frame rebate 3.6. What is the mean of the four readings?
questions.explanation: The four readings sum to 11.0, and dividing that by the four measurements gives a mean of 2.75. The low reading at the centre pulls the mean well below the readings around the edges.
questions.hint: Add the four readings and divide by four.

stimulus.body: The note records that a drawing was made on a linen canvas whose weave is 12 threads per centimetre, and that the lines run cleanly across the threads with no interruption, while a companion study on a smooth panel of the same size is drawn in a broken, sketchy line.

options.misconception: claims a heavier tool is required on canvas

options.text: It forces the artist to draw a broken line, because the threads catch the point.
options.misconception: claims the canvas always breaks the line

options.misconception: denies the support any effect on the drawing

options.text: It allows a clean continuous line, whereas the smooth panel produces the broken sketchy line.

questions.explanation: The note shows the weave giving a clean line while the smooth support produced the broken one, so the support changes how a stroke reads. A fixed rule, no effect and a heavier tool contradict the record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a warm ground alters the colours painted above it
questions.stem: A survey team member asks in writing how a warm ground alters the colours painted above it.

answer.exemplar: A warm imprimatura is a thin tinted layer applied over the ground before the picture is painted, and because it lies under the paint it shows through every passage that was not laid thickly. Warm tones gain from it, since the added warmth brings the mixture towards the same family, while cool tones are pulled towards it and can be turned greyer or duller than the painter intended, which is why the choice of ground is part of the palette decision.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the ground sits beneath the paint and alters thin passages by showing through. It should not describe the imprimatura as a final glaze or as a purely decorative ground.
questions.hint: Say where the imprimatura sits in the build-up.

options.text: The original paint has yellowed unevenly, because the ground beneath was of variable quality.
options.misconception: blames the ground for uneven yellowing

options.text: A later varnish has been applied unevenly, settling in hollows and on upward-facing edges.
The panel has been varnished twice, and the two coats have merged into one cloud.
options.misconception: reads cloudiness as two merged varnish coats

options.text: The picture has been cleaned with an abrasive, which has left a hazy film on the surface.
options.misconception: blames abrasive cleaning for the haze

questions.explanation: A layer that gathers in hollows and on upward edges has flowed or been brushed over a long period, typical of a later varnish. Uneven ground, merged coats and abrasive cleaning would not follow the relief like this.
questions.hint: Ask where a flowing liquid would collect.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish cracks in the film from cracks in the support
questions.stem: A surveyor must decide whether a crack pattern belongs to the paint film or to the wooden support, given that the cracks run across the grain and open at the joints.

options.text: Treating them as a recent impact, because support splits spread outward from a blow.
options.misconception: assumes support splits radiate from an impact

options.text: Treating them as age cracks in the film, because film cracks never follow the grain.
options.misconception: claims film cracks never follow the grain

options.text: Treating them as splits in the support, because they follow the grain and open at the joints.
Treating them as insect damage, because the larvae of wood borers follow the grain.
options.misconception: explains the pattern as insect damage

questions.explanation: Cracks that follow the grain and open at the joints belong to the wood, since the film breaks where the board breaks. Film cracks ignoring the grain, an impact and insect damage do not match this pattern.
questions.hint: Follow the grain and look at the joints.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: List the physical signs by which a later varnish is recognised
questions.stem: A survey protocol asks in writing how a later varnish can be recognised on a panel.

answer.exemplar: A varnish applied after the artist has left the object tends to be uneven in thickness, collecting in hollows, along edges and in the recesses of raised work, and it takes on a yellow or amber tone of its own. Where the picture has been handled, the later film is thinned or removed, so the surface shows a mixture of protected and exposed areas. Its tint also sits above the paint rather than being part of it, which is why the film can be seen to lie on the picture.

questions.explanation: A good answer lists uneven thickness, a yellow tint, wear at handled points and the fact that the film lies above the paint. It should not claim the later varnish can be dated from its colour alone.
questions.hint: List the physical signs the survey team can record.

questions.explanation: A transparent second film over an opaque colour is a glaze, and the changed return of light from the layers below is what gives depth. More pigment, thick varnish and skill would not produce a transparent film.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a canvas support changes the drawing
questions.learningObjective: Describe the mechanism by which a woven support breaks a line
questions.stem: A drawing instructor asks in writing how a woven support changes the character of a line.

answer.exemplar: A woven support offers a grid of high and low points, and a point dragged across it catches in the hollows and skates over the crowns, so a line laid down with any pressure at all will break into a chain of short marks. The same gesture on a smooth prepared panel gives a continuous line, and the difference between the two is not a difference in skill but in what the tool meets.

questions.explanation: A good answer describes the mechanism by which the weave interrupts a stroke and contrasts it with a smooth support. It should not attribute the difference to care, talent or a change of instrument.
questions.hint: Describe what the tool meets on the way across.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same mixture reads differently over different grounds
questions.stem: A survey compares a panel with a warm brown ground and a second with a cool grey ground. The same flesh colour is mixed for both, and it appears noticeably pinker on the warm ground and greyer on the cool one.

options.text: The cool ground is a modern overpaint, which has drained the warmth from the flesh.
options.misconception: suggests the cool ground is an overpaint

options.text: The warm ground is a later addition, and the flesh colour was originally mixed to suit it.
options.misconception: blames the warm ground for being a later addition

options.text: The two flesh colours were mixed differently, since a painter never mixes the same colour twice.
options.misconception: insists the mixtures must differ

options.text: The ground shows through the thin flesh colour and shifts its hue, so the two grounds read differently.

questions.explanation: A thin flesh mixture lets the ground beneath alter its hue, so the same mixture reads pinker on a warm ground. A later addition, different mixtures and an overpaint are not needed to explain a consistent shift between two grounds.
questions.hint: Consider how thin the flesh layer is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a glaze produces depth of colour
questions.learningObjective: Locate where a change in a glazed passage is actually located
questions.stem: A surveyor must advise a curator whose panel has a glaze that is turning cloudy, with the colour beneath still bright and unaltered.

options.text: Advising that the whole panel is affected, so the picture must be cleaned and re-varnished as one.
options.misconception: advises treating the entire panel as affected

options.text: Advising that the glaze alone has altered, so it can be removed and renewed without touching the picture.
Advising that nothing should be done, because a cloudy glaze is part of the original picture.
options.misconception: treats the cloudiness as original to the picture

options.text: Advising that more glaze be added, building a thicker film over the clouding one.
options.misconception: advises adding more glaze over a cloudy one

questions.explanation: A cloudy glaze over a sound picture is a surface problem confined to the glaze, so it can be worked on alone. Treating the whole panel, leaving it and adding a further film all miss where the change lies.
questions.hint: Locate the change before choosing a treatment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a network of fine cracks in a painted sky indicates
questions.stem: A surveyor asks what the pattern of a network of fine cracks across a panel's painted sky tells the team.

options.text: That the panel was damaged by heat, since heat alone makes networks of cracks.
options.misconception: attributes the network to heat damage

options.text: That the wood behind the panel has split in several places.
options.misconception: reads a fine network as splits in the wood

options.text: That the film has aged and shrunk over a support that stayed fairly stable.
That the picture was painted with a drying medium that cracked as it cured.
options.misconception: blames the paint medium for the cracking

questions.explanation: A regular network of fine cells over the paint and absent at the edges points to an aged film shrinking on a stable support. Splits in the wood, heat and a drying medium would each leave a different pattern.
questions.hint: Compare the edges with the painted field.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the variation in thickness of a varnish film
questions.stem: A survey team gauges the varnish film on a panel at 0.018 mm in the hollow of a fold and 0.006 mm on the flat field. By how much does the film differ between the two readings?
questions.explanation: The film is thicker in the hollow by 0.018 minus 0.006, which is 0.012 mm. Such a difference over a short distance is the sign of a film that has run and settled over time.
questions.hint: Subtract the thinner reading from the thicker.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Interpret crack size in relation to the thickness of the paint

stimulus.body: The sheet records that on one panel the cracks form a dense mesh of small cells across the sky and the flesh, that the mesh is finer in the thinly painted passages, and that the panel's wooden edges show no cracking at all.

questions.stem: According to the condition sheet, what does the difference in crack size between passages indicate?

options.text: That the paint was applied in a colder studio, which shrinks it unevenly.
options.misconception: blames studio temperature for the crack size

options.text: That the thinly painted passages were executed by a different and less skilled hand.
options.misconception: blames a different hand for the thinner passages

options.text: That the wooden edges were replaced, since real wood never cracks in this pattern.
options.misconception: suggests the edges were replaced

options.text: That the film shrinks and cracks by different amounts according to how thick and loaded it is.

questions.explanation: A mesh that changes in scale with paint thickness shows a film responding to its own load and to the amount of binder it holds. A different hand, replaced edges and a cold studio would not tie crack size to passage thickness.
questions.hint: Relate the crack size to the thickness of the paint.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pentimento evidences
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a surviving earlier version matters to the record
questions.stem: A survey report asks in writing why an earlier version showing through a painting matters to the record.

answer.exemplar: An earlier version that survives beneath a later one proves that the artist worked the picture in stages and revised it in the course of doing so, and it can reveal the first intention of a passage before a covering layer hid it. In records of panel painting this is a valuable fixed point, because it is a dated, physical trace of a decision that the finished image alone would have concealed.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that a surviving earlier version evidences revision during the work and provides a physical trace of an original intention. It should not treat it as a separate painting or a signature.
questions.hint: Say what the trace fixes in the record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an applied film from an aged paint layer
questions.stem: A survey panel shows two different surface effects: the paint layer itself is crazed, while a separate, smoother and slightly yellow film lies over the whole panel and is thicker around the edges.

options.text: The panel is uniformly old, and the difference in appearance is simply a difference of viewing light.
options.misconception: blames the viewing light for the two effects

options.text: The panel carries an applied film over an aged paint layer, and the two have aged differently.
The panel was repainted, and the film over it is a later varnish on the new paint.
options.misconception: assumes the picture was repainted

options.text: The smooth film is a modern plastic sheet laid over the panel for protection.
options.misconception: suggests a modern plastic covering

questions.explanation: A crazed paint layer under a separate smooth film shows an applied layer that has aged apart from the picture. Uniform ageing, a repainting and a plastic sheet would not leave the two effects separated.
questions.hint: Look for two distinct layers rather than one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: Decide what a survey record must include about a showing ground
questions.stem: A curator asks a surveyor how to record a panel whose ground colour has become visible in thin passages and is now influencing the picture.

options.text: Record the varnish instead, because the varnish is what carries the ground's colour.
options.misconception: claims the varnish carries the ground colour

options.text: Record only the finished colours, since the ground beneath is not part of the picture.
options.misconception: dismisses the ground as irrelevant to the record

options.text: Record the ground colour and the areas where it shows through, so the shift can be described.
Record nothing, because the ground cannot be seen in the finished picture.
options.misconception: claims the ground cannot be seen at all

questions.explanation: A survey record of a panel has to include the ground and where it shows through, since that is exactly what now governs the colour of the thin passages. Ignoring the ground, blaming the varnish and recording nothing all miss the mechanism.
questions.hint: The ground is part of the picture's behaviour.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sfumato changes in a face
questions.learningObjective: Identify a dissolved boundary between shadow and light
questions.stem: A survey team notes a portrait in which no line marks the boundary of the shadow on the neck.

options.text: The varnish has run down the neck and blurred the paint beneath it.
options.misconception: blames running varnish for the soft edge

options.text: The shadow has been omitted, so the neck is lighter than the rest of the face.
options.misconception: reads the soft edge as an omitted shadow

options.text: The neck was left unfinished and is now covered by a later grey layer.
options.misconception: treats the soft edge as an unfinished passage

options.text: The boundary between the shadow and the light has been dissolved into a soft transition.

questions.explanation: A boundary that has been dissolved into a soft transition is the defining feature of sfumato, where the tone itself carries the form. An omitted shadow, an unfinished passage and running varnish would each look different.
questions.hint: The shadow is present, only its edge is not.

questions.topic: How a canvas support changes the drawing
questions.learningObjective: Count the threads of a woven support in a measured field
questions.stem: A surveyor counts the threads of a linen canvas in a 1 cm field and finds 12 in one direction and 10 in the other. How many threads are there in total in that 1 cm field?
questions.explanation: The two directions give 12 and 10 threads in the same 1 cm field, and together they make 22. Counting the field along one direction only would miss the cross threads.
questions.hint: Add the counts in the two directions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a glaze produces depth of colour
questions.learningObjective: Explain how glazing and rubbing back build depth in a passage

stimulus.body: The record notes that a pale blue passage was first painted in opaque colour, then covered with a thin layer of deep blue, and that the surface was then rubbed back in the lights, so that the lighter colour shows in the highlights while the deep layer remains in the shadows.

questions.stem: According to the record, how does the glazing and rubbing back produce the effect?

options.text: The deep layer is simply left to cover the pale colour everywhere, hiding it completely.
options.misconception: assumes the glaze hides the pale colour entirely

options.text: The deep layer deepens the shadowed passages while the rubbed lights return to the colour beneath.
The rubbing back exposes a primer of the same deep blue, giving a uniform colour.
options.misconception: claims the rubbing exposed a primer

options.text: The pale colour is repainted over the lights, so the glaze has no effect on the result.
options.misconception: suggests the effect comes from repainting

questions.explanation: The record describes a deep layer that stays in the shadows while the lights are cut back to the colour beneath, which is how depth is built by glazing. A uniform cover, a primer and a repaint would each give a different account.
questions.hint: Notice what the lights show and what the shadows show.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a varnish must be recorded as part of the object's history
questions.stem: A survey protocol asks in writing why varnish has to be recorded even when it is not part of the artist's picture.

answer.exemplar: A varnish is a layer laid on the picture by somebody, often long after the artist, and it changes the surface dramatically, deepening the colour and adding a gloss that was never in the painting itself. It also gathers dirt, darkens and becomes brittle, and it is frequently renewed or removed, so a survey that ignored it would misdate the surface, misread the colour and miss a large part of the object's history.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that varnish alters the surface, ages, is renewed and belongs to the object's later history. It should not treat varnish as part of the original picture or as a protective layer that never changes.
questions.hint: Ask who applied it and what it does to the colour.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Compare the crack networks of two panels of different ages
questions.stem: A survey compares two panels of the same workshop. On the older one the crack network is fine and dense; on the newer one it is coarse and open, and a few cells have lifted away from the support.

options.text: The newer panel was stored in a hot room, and heat alone widens every crack.
options.misconception: attributes the coarse cracks to heat

options.text: The newer panel was painted with an inferior medium, which cracks into coarse cells.
options.misconception: blames an inferior medium for coarse cracking

options.text: The older film has had longer to shrink and dry, which produces a finer and more crowded network.
The newer panel was lined with a coarse cloth, and the weave shows through the cracks.
options.misconception: suggests a coarse lining caused the cracks

questions.explanation: A fine crowded network in the older film is what long drying produces, and coarse open cells belong to a younger film beginning to fail. An inferior medium, heat and a lining do not follow the age order.
questions.hint: Compare the two panels by age.

questions.topic: How a canvas support changes the drawing
questions.learningObjective: Advise on reading a drawing on a distorted support
questions.stem: A surveyor must advise on a drawing on linen that has been stored rolled, where the creases have broken the lines and the weave has distorted.

options.text: Recommending that the drawing be transferred to a panel before anything is recorded.
options.misconception: proposes transfer before recording

options.text: Recommending that the drawing be read from the creases, since they show the artist's changes.
options.misconception: reads the creases as the artist's corrections

options.text: Recommending that the drawing be cleaned with solvent, which will relax the weave.
options.misconception: believes solvent will relax a distorted weave

options.text: Recommending that the support be flattened and supported before any attempt is made to read the drawing.

questions.explanation: A distorted support distorts the strokes on it, so it must be stabilised before the drawing can be read. Creases as changes, solvent cleaning and transfer all treat the drawing, not the cause.
questions.hint: Stabilise the support before reading the marks.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the presence of a glaze from a depth record
questions.stem: A survey note records a passage of the picture where the colour looks deeper and more transparent than the pigment used could produce alone.

options.text: The colour was mixed with a darker pigment than the pigment record names.
options.misconception: assumes the pigment was mixed darker

options.text: A transparent layer of a deeper colour has been laid over the first, deepening it.
The panel was waxed, and wax deepens the colour of every pigment beneath it.
options.misconception: blames wax for deepening the colour

options.text: The passage was varnished, and varnish deepens the colours it covers.
options.misconception: blames varnish for the depth

questions.explanation: Depth that exceeds the pigment record points to a transparent deeper layer over the first, which is a glaze. A darker mix, wax and varnish do not produce the transparent second film a glaze is.
questions.hint: What can make a colour deeper without more pigment?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Convert a measured crack width back to the size on the panel
questions.stem: A surveyor measures the width of crack cells in a photograph taken at 4x magnification. The average cell measures 0.4 mm in the image. What is the average cell width on the actual panel?
questions.explanation: A measurement taken at 4x magnification is four times the true size, so the real width is 0.4 divided by 4, which is 0.1 mm. Failing to divide would overstate the cell size fourfold.
questions.hint: Divide the measured width by the magnification.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an imprimatura does to hue
questions.learningObjective: Attribute a change in hue to a documented intervention

stimulus.body: The history records that the panel was cleaned down to the ground in 1958, that a warm brown wash was then applied over the whole field, and that the figures were repainted over it. Photographs from 1955 show the same flesh passages distinctly cool, and the present surface reads distinctly warm.

questions.stem: According to the restoration history, what accounts for the change in the flesh passages?

options.text: The panel was lit more warmly during the 1955 photography than it is now.
options.misconception: blames the photographic lighting

options.text: The flesh passages were repainted with a warmer pigment than the original painter used.
options.misconception: blames a warmer pigment in the repaint

options.text: The warm wash now shows through the thin repainted flesh, pulling it towards warmth.
The ground has darkened with age, which by itself warms every colour above it.
options.misconception: claims a darkening ground warms the paint above it

questions.explanation: The cool-to-warm change follows the addition of the warm wash, because thin flesh paint lets the layer beneath show through. A warmer pigment, photographic lighting and age alone do not tie the shift to the documented intervention.
questions.hint: What was added in 1958?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a crack pattern is recorded before cleaning
questions.stem: A survey report asks in writing why the pattern of cracks should be recorded before a panel is cleaned.

answer.exemplar: The crack network is a record of how the film has aged on its support, and cleaning dissolves the varnish that holds the flakes in place, so the pattern that was there is lifted away before it has been described. Recording it first also lets a later restorer compare the pattern with the ground and support beneath, and can warn that the film is already failing and needs consolidating rather than further cleaning.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that cleaning removes the evidence and that a record made first supports later treatment decisions. It should not claim that cracks prove a particular artist or a particular date.
questions.hint: Cleaning takes the evidence with it.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a painted form crossed by an earlier outline
questions.stem: A survey records a panel on which a painted wing of a bird is crossed by a faint curve that matches the outline of a wing in the layer beneath.

options.text: The faint curve is a watermark from the paper of an old drawing used as padding.
options.misconception: explains the curve as a paper watermark

options.text: The picture has been varnished over a crack that happens to look like a wing.
options.misconception: reads the curve as a crack in the varnish

options.text: The panel was made from two boards, and the joint has copied a wing shape.
options.misconception: suggests the joint copied the wing

options.text: The artist painted a bird over a first, different wing, so the earlier shape survives beneath.

questions.explanation: A painted form crossed by a different outline beneath is a change made during the work, with the older one surviving under the newer. A varnish crack, a joint and a paper watermark would not align so exactly.
questions.hint: Ask which shape was painted first.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a safe approach to a degraded varnish layer
questions.stem: A survey team must decide how to handle a panel whose varnish is thick, yellow and slightly sticky, and whose paint beneath is sound and matt.

options.text: Recommending that more varnish be added to stiffen the sticky film and stop it moving.
options.misconception: advises adding varnish over a sticky film

options.text: Recommending that the varnish be removed by a conservator, tested first on a small area.
Recommending that the panel be scrubbed with solvent until the yellow layer is gone.
options.misconception: advises scrubbing a sound paint layer

options.text: Recommending that the panel be left, because a sticky varnish is the mark of a well-made picture.
options.misconception: treats the sticky varnish as a sign of quality

questions.explanation: A thick, degraded varnish over sound matt paint is a surface problem for a conservator, and the first move is a controlled test on a small area. More varnish, scrubbing and leaving a sticky film all risk the picture beneath.
questions.hint: Test on a small area before treating the whole.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an applied film from its angle-dependent shine

options.misconception: insists wax is the only cause of shine

options.text: The paint itself was mixed with a high gloss varnish medium by the artist.
options.misconception: blames the artist's paint medium for the shine

options.text: A film lies on the picture and reflects light, which is what a varnish does.
The glass of the display case is reflecting the lamp onto the panel.
options.misconception: blames case glass for the shine

questions.topic: What a sfumato changes in a face
questions.learningObjective: Locate the softened passage described in a conservation note

stimulus.body: The note describes a head in a portrait where the edge of the hair meets the forehead without a break, and where the value of the hair continues into the value of the shadow on the forehead. The line of the jaw is the only hard edge in the passage.

questions.stem: According to the note, which part of the head shows the effect of sfumato?

options.text: The neck, where the shadow is darkest and therefore most distinct.
options.misconception: mistakes a dark shadow for a soft edge

options.text: The line of the jaw, where the edge is drawn sharply against the neck.
options.misconception: identifies the hard jaw edge as the softened passage

options.text: The whole head, since a soft effect applies evenly to every passage.
options.misconception: claims the softening is uniform over the head

options.text: The meeting of the hair and the forehead, where the tone passes from one to the other.

questions.explanation: The note distinguishes the softened meeting of hair and forehead from the one hard edge at the jaw, so the effect is local and deliberate. A uniform softening, the jaw and the darkest shadow all misread the description.
questions.hint: The note names one hard edge. Find the rest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a canvas support changes the drawing
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a support must be accounted for in describing a drawing
questions.stem: A survey manual asks in writing how a conservator should account for the support when describing a drawing.

answer.exemplar: A drawing on a woven support cannot be described as though it were on a smooth one, because the tool meets a grid of high and low points and the stroke is interrupted at every thread. A drawing made with a dragging point, a blunt one and a flexible one will all break differently on canvas. The record should therefore name the support and its weave, and describe the marks as marks made on that support.

questions.explanation: A good answer insists that the support and its weave are part of what the drawing is, and that the marks must be described on that support. It should not treat the drawing as independent of what it was drawn on.
questions.hint: The support is part of the drawing.

options.text: A single red pigment mixed with more oil is producing the range in one layer.
options.misconception: explains the range by a single mixed pigment

options.text: A transparent dark glaze over a light colour is producing the range between the lights and the shadows.
A later repaint has darkened the shadows, leaving the original lights visible.
options.misconception: suggests the shadows were repainted

options.text: The range comes from a yellow varnish over the red, warming the lights.
options.misconception: blames varnish for the range of values

questions.explanation: Two films with a clear range of value between the lights and shadows is the working of a glaze over an opaque colour. A single mixed pigment, a repaint and a yellow varnish would each leave a different number of films.
questions.hint: The gauge counted two films.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a fine crack network needs urgent treatment
questions.stem: A survey lead must decide whether a fine crack network on a panel needs a treatment, given that the flakes still lie flat and the paint is firmly attached.

options.text: Deciding that it proves a recent impact and that the panel must be rebuilt.
options.misconception: reads stable cracks as impact damage

options.text: Deciding that it is serious and that the whole film must be consolidated at once.
options.misconception: calls stable cracks a reason for urgent consolidation

options.text: Deciding that it is a stable age crack and that no immediate treatment is needed.
Deciding that the network proves an earlier repaint and that the picture is a copy.
options.misconception: treats the crack network as proof of a copy

questions.explanation: Cracks whose flakes lie flat and remain firmly attached describe a film that has aged but not failed, so nothing urgent is needed. Rebuilding, urgent consolidation and a claim about repainting all exceed what the survey shows.
questions.hint: Ask whether any flake is lifting.

options.misconception: mistakes the imprimatura for a varnish

options.text: The wash was applied at the end and deepened the finished colours.
options.misconception: places the imprimatura after the painting

options.text: The wash replaced the ground, so the picture has no ground beneath it at all.
options.misconception: claims the wash replaced the ground

options.text: The wash sat beneath the paint and altered the hue of every thin passage above it.

questions.explanation: An imprimatura is a tinted layer laid on the ground before painting, so it changes the colour of the thin paint above it. A final wash, a replacement ground and a varnish are all different operations.
questions.hint: Where in the build-up does it sit?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sfumato changes in a face
questions.learningObjective: Compare the tonal gradients of a hard edge and a soft edge
questions.stem: A survey photograph is examined with a densitometer. Across a softened edge the tone changes by 12 units over 8 mm, and across a hard edge it changes by 12 units over 1 mm. How many times steeper is the hard edge in tonal change per millimetre?
questions.explanation: The hard edge changes 12 units per millimetre and the soft edge 12 over 8 millimetres, which is 1.5 units per millimetre. Twelve divided by 1.5 gives a factor of 8 for the hard edge.
questions.hint: Compare the two gradients as a ratio.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a craquelure pattern indicates
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change in a crack network over time

stimulus.body: The note records that a painting stored in a warm, damp store shows a crack network whose cells are noticeably larger and more widely spaced than the network recorded on the same panel three years earlier, and that the paint has begun to lift at one corner.

questions.stem: According to the monitoring note, what does the change in the crack network indicate?

options.text: That the panel has been repainted, since a new network always forms in three years.
options.misconception: explains the change as a repainting

options.text: That the film is still moving, so the network is widening and the panel needs attention.
That the panel is improving, since a wider network shows the film settling.
options.misconception: reads widening cracks as an improvement

options.text: That the earlier record was mistaken, because crack networks never change.
options.misconception: claims crack networks never change

questions.explanation: A network that has widened since the last survey shows a film that is still under strain, and the lifting corner confirms it. A repainting, an improvement and an error in the earlier record do not account for measured change over time.
questions.hint: Compare the two records of the same panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a later varnish gives itself away
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a later varnish permanently alters a picture's appearance
questions.stem: A survey report asks in writing why a later varnish sometimes changes the appearance of a picture for good.

answer.exemplar: A later varnish is usually chosen for its clarity and its yellowing, and it fills the fine texture of a dry paint film, which deepens the colour and adds a gloss the artist never applied. Once that film is on, the depth and the warmth of the picture are altered in a way that cannot be reversed by cleaning, and the varnish itself will darken further and become brittle, so each later campaign adds another layer to the record.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the later varnish permanently changes the surface and adds to the record. It should not claim a later varnish can be removed without any effect on the picture.
questions.hint: Say what the film does to the surface it covers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a pentimento evidences
questions.learningObjective: Read two cloud positions as a revised design
questions.stem: A survey panel shows, beneath a finished sky, a second set of clouds drawn in a lighter chalky line, offset from the painted ones and partly covered by them.

options.text: The chalky line is a later addition made to show a repair to the panel.
options.misconception: treats the lighter line as a modern repair mark

options.text: The painted clouds are a copy of a print, and the chalky line is a tracing guide.
options.misconception: explains the underdrawing as a copy from a print

options.text: A sky with clouds was first drawn and then covered by a revised sky with the clouds in a new position.
The panel was made from two pieces, and the line marks where they were joined.
options.misconception: explains the line as a panel join

questions.explanation: Two cloud positions, one drawn and one painted with the drawing partly covered, record a design that was changed. A copied print, a modern repair mark and a panel join describe the picture's making, not its revision.
questions.hint: Ask which clouds were painted and which were only drawn.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a canvas support changes the drawing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a drawing on linen can read fuller than one on a panel
questions.stem: A surveyor comparing a drawing on linen with one on a prepared panel finds that the linen version is fuller and more broken in tone.

options.text: The canvas was made larger, and the extra size makes the drawing look fuller.
options.misconception: links the fuller look to the size of the support

options.text: The linen was painted with more pigment, so the tone is naturally fuller.
options.misconception: blames the amount of pigment for the fuller tone

options.text: The canvas was lined with a soft cloth, which adds depth to the drawing.
options.misconception: suggests a soft lining adds depth

options.text: The weave catches the medium, so the tone is broken up and appears fuller on the canvas.

questions.explanation: A weave breaks the medium into a broken tone, which reads as a fuller and more textured drawing than the same work on a smooth panel. More pigment, a soft lining and a larger support do not explain a broken tone.
questions.hint: Think about what the threads do to the medium.
